day_context.today_label: Matchday 10 — the champions come to call
day_context.tournament_summary: Brazil meet Haiti in Philadelphia, and the fixture carries a memory most of the world has forgotten. In 2004, Brazil's world champions flew to Port-au-Prince during a Brazilian-led UN peacekeeping mission and played a 'Match for Peace' tied to a weapons-surrender drive — a million people are said to have lined the streets. Twenty-two years later Haiti are no longer the hosts of a goodwill visit but opponents at a World Cup, back at the tournament for the first time since their lone appearance in 1974. Around the marquee: the Netherlands face Sweden in Houston, Germany meet Ivory Coast in Toronto in a first-ever encounter, and Türkiye take on Paraguay in the Bay Area.
context_notes: Brazil vs Haiti at Lincoln Financial Field, Philadelphia — the two have never met at a World Cup; their famous meeting was the 2004 'Match for Peace' friendly in Port-au-Prince.
Haiti's only previous World Cup was 1974 (lost all three: Italy 3-1, Poland 7-0, Argentina 4-1); 2026 is their return.
Netherlands vs Sweden at NRG Stadium, Houston — they have met once at a World Cup, a 0-0 draw in 1974.
Germany vs Ivory Coast at BMO Field, Toronto — their first-ever World Cup meeting and only their second meeting of any kind (a 2-2 friendly in 2009).
Türkiye vs Paraguay at Levi's Stadium, San Francisco Bay Area.

here_there_thread.topic: Port-au-Prince and Brazil — the day the world champions came under a blue helmet
here_there_thread.framing: Long before this World Cup fixture, Brazil and Haiti shared one of football's strangest afternoons: a friendly that doubled as a peace operation. The thread runs from a battered stadium in Port-au-Prince in 2004 to a sold-out NFL ground in Philadelphia in 2026 — same two flags, opposite circumstances.

facts.label: Port-au-Prince, 18 Aug 2004
facts.fact: Brazil's world champions played a 'Match for Peace' (Jogo da Paz) at the Stade Sylvio Cator, during the Brazilian-led UN Stabilisation Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH) set up earlier that year.

facts.label: Guns for tickets
facts.fact: The match was tied to a disarmament drive: some tickets were exchanged for surrendered weapons, letting fans watch the champions while contributing to the gesture.

facts.label: The parade
facts.fact: Brazil's squad rode through the city atop UN and Brazilian-Army armoured vehicles to reach the stadium, drawing crowds estimated up to a million; Brazil won the match 6-0, Ronaldinho scoring three.

facts.label: The recognition
facts.fact: Brazil's federation received FIFA's Fair Play Award for 2004 for the match's humanitarian impact — presented at the ceremony where Ronaldinho was named World Player of the Year.

facts.label: Now
facts.fact: In 2026 the roles invert: Haiti arrive in Philadelphia not as hosts of a goodwill visit but as opponents at a World Cup, on Brazil's side of the draw rather than the receiving end of its charity.

story_behind_number.surface_stat: Dino Zoff · 1,142 minutes unbeaten — ended by Haiti
story_behind_number.historical_anchor: At the 1974 World Cup — Haiti's only appearance before this one — Italy's goalkeeper Dino Zoff carried a world-record run of 1,142 minutes without conceding for his country. Forty-six seconds into the second half of Haiti's opener, Emmanuel 'Manno' Sanon ran onto a Philippe Vorbé through-ball and beat Zoff. The record was gone. Italy recovered to win 3-1, but the goal outlived the result: a debutant nation's striker ending one of the game's great streaks.

quick_facts.v: Dino Zoff, 1,142 minutes unbeaten for Italy — a world record at the time
Manno Sanon, 46', off a Philippe Vorbé pass — Haiti 1-0 up against the 1970 finalists
Olympiastadion, Munich; Italy rallied to win 3-1 (Rivera, Benetti, Anastasi)
Their only prior World Cup; they lost all three but Sanon's goal is the one everyone remembers

supporting_context: Sanon's strike is one of the enduring images of the 1974 tournament — a player from a debutant island beating the world's best goalkeeper at his peak.
It is the thread that connects this Haiti to its history: 52 years on (a gap told elsewhere), the number that travels with them is 1,142 — the streak they broke.
Brazil arrive as five-time champions; Haiti arrive with one immortal goal and the knowledge that World Cups are where their nation has, just once, touched greatness.

from_the_stands.question: My father grew up on the story of Sanon's goal against Zoff in '74 — it's the reason our family watches football at all. Now we're back, and it's Brazil. What does a 'good day' realistically look like for Haiti against the five-time champions — is there any version of this we walk away from proud?

facts: Haiti's World Cup history is one immortal moment, not a body of results: Sanon's 1974 goal that ended Zoff's 1,142-minute streak, inside a campaign where they lost all three games.

Brazil are five-time champions and heavy favourites; the two have never met at a World Cup, and their non-WC meetings have been lopsided (a 7-1 Copa América win in 2016, the 6-0 'Match for Peace' in 2004).
But the 48-team format rewards a single good performance: eight of the best third-placed teams advance, so a debutant-class side can lose to the group's giant and still progress.
A 'good day' for Haiti is measurable without a win — staying compact, scoring (as Sanon did), and keeping the goal difference survivable for the games against beatable opponents.
factual_brief.note: The question asks whether pride is possible against Brazil. The brief reframes 'a good day': in the old 32-team format only winning your group mattered; now a competitive loss plus a goal can keep Haiti alive on the third-place route. Pride and progress are no longer mutually exclusive.

anomalies.tag: The match that disarmed a city
anomalies.seed: Brazil and Haiti's most famous meeting wasn't a World Cup game at all: the 2004 'Match for Peace' in Port-au-Prince, played under a Brazilian-led UN mission with tickets swapped for surrendered weapons and the world champions paraded through the streets atop armoured vehicles. Brazil won 6-0; the gesture won FIFA's Fair Play Award.

Haiti's defining World Cup moment is 52 years old: Manno Sanon's 1974 goal that ended Dino Zoff's record 1,142-minute unbeaten run for Italy. It is the one time a debutant island beat the best goalkeeper alive — and it still travels with them.

The Netherlands meet Sweden in Houston for only the second time at a World Cup; their first was a 0-0 draw in 1974 — the same tournament, that same summer, where Sanon was breaking Zoff's record a few groups over.
Germany and Ivory Coast meet at a World Cup for the very first time, in Toronto — only the second meeting of any kind between the four-time champions and the Elephants, after a 2-2 friendly in 2009.
